The three regimes—purposive selection, coordinated influence, and stochastic chance—are foundational to organic stability. Purposive selection implies directed optimization, often modeled via gradient descent or similar deterministic mechanisms. Coordinated influence reflects complex feedback loops, akin to networked dynamical systems where each node is influenced by multiple others. Stochastic chance introduces randomness, typically captured through probabilistic models or noise-driven processes. These regimes form a triadic structure that governs how biological systems evolve and stabilize. Failure modes arise when one regime dominates excessively—e.g., over-reliance on purposeful control leads to rigidity, while excessive stochasticity results in instability. The interplay between these domains defines the robustness of an organism or system. Dualities emerge in the transition from deterministic to probabilistic behavior, especially at phase boundaries. For instance, the boundary between ordered and chaotic dynamics mirrors the shift from purposive to accidental influence. Each regime contributes distinct information to the overall system state, enabling both predictive modeling and adaptive response strategies.
